title: A 10-million-year biogeographic holding pen primed the Great American Biotic Interchange.
data_url: https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.aef2893 (supplementary Data S1 to S8; publisher-hosted only)

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Extracted the full accepted manuscript text from the author's eScholarship PDF (7 pages) and read its data-availability statement, acknowledgments and record counts. Probed for the data in four places: Dryad application programming interface (0 hits for this DOI), Zenodo (no matching deposit), Europe PMC (article is not open access, has no PubMed Central identifier, so no supplementary-file listing), and the Paleobiology Database (PBDB, the open global fossil occurrence archive) application programming interface, which returns 639 Neogene mammal occurrences for Mexico and 16,224 for the United States. Both science.org pages (article and guessed supplementary-file path) returned HTTP 403 to automated requests.
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: All record counts (1,724 unique genus-locality records for Mexico, up from 919; 1,920 for South America; 2,296 for temperate North America), the list of supplementary items (Figs. S1-S15, Tables S1-S5, Data S1-S8), the column content of those data files, and the statement that specimen catalog numbers live in data S2. I never saw a single row of the actual data.

a1_downloadable.note: The data exists only as Science supplementary files (Data S1 to S8) on a paywalled, bot-blocked publisher site: 'All data are available in the main text or the supplementary materials', with no repository deposit, no code link, and no PubMed Central copy. Dryad and Zenodo searches returned nothing, and the new Mexican records are not in the Paleobiology Database (PBDB still holds 639 Mexico Neogene mammal occurrences, matching the paper's own pre-study figure of 640, versus the 1,724 records the paper claims to have compiled).

a2_label_is_a_column.note: From the paper text only: the files are fossil occurrence records (taxon, locality, age, region). Any prediction target here (did a genus disperse south, when did it arrive, how long did it sit in the holding pen) must be constructed by inferring first and last appearances across records and regions.

a3_inputs_present.note: From the paper text only: the obvious predictors of dispersal (body mass, diet, locomotion) are not in the occurrence table and would have to be joined in from outside trait resources such as the Mammal Diversity Database or published body-mass compilations, genus by genus.

a4_units_stated.note: Ages are in millions of years ago and stable carbon isotope values in per mil, both stated unambiguously in the text; not checked in the files because the files are unavailable.

a5_enough_rows.note: Paper text gives 1,724 + 1,920 + 2,296 = 5,940 genus-locality records, but the biological unit for any dispersal model is the genus, and the paper's own figures count 21 to 136 genera per region and interval - far below the ~1,500 rows a regression needs or the ~400 a classifier needs.

a6_fits_laptop.note: Tiny tabular data by construction; size is the one thing that is clearly fine, inferred from record counts rather than from an opened file.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: The only count I could cross-check matched: the paper says 640 Mexican Neogene mammal occurrences in PBDB as of October 2025, and PBDB returns 639 today. The paper's own 1,724 records could not be checked against any download.

a8_label_provenance.note: Occurrences rest on physical specimens with museum catalog numbers at the Instituto de Geociencias (UNAM), and ages on biochronology, magnetostratigraphy and isotope work, so nothing is another model's output - judged from the paper text only.

existing_models.name: DES (dispersal-extinction-sampling) model, a Bayesian method that infers dispersal and extinction rates directly from fossil occurrences while correcting for incomplete sampling
existing_models.score_and_split: Not a predictive classifier, so no held-out score; published as a method in Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B (retrieved via search, PubMed Central identifier PMC4810818).
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Not read in full - only the search summary, which states the method addresses fossil-record incompleteness.

existing_models.name: Trait-dependent DES extension (Hauffe and colleagues, 2022, Methods in Ecology and Evolution), which estimates how traits, diversity and environment affect fossil dispersal and extinction rates
existing_models.score_and_split: Method paper, no prediction benchmark; retrieved as a search result only (abstract page, not full text).

existing_models.name: DeepDive, a deep-learning model that estimates biodiversity through time from simulated fossil records and regional occurrence data
existing_models.score_and_split: Evaluated on simulated diversity trajectories rather than a held-out empirical split, per the retrieved summary (PubMed Central identifier PMC11101433).

backbone.name: None applicable - fossil occurrence tables are not sequence, molecule, image or single-cell data, so no pretrained backbone (ESM-2, ChemBERTa, DNABERT-2 and similar) fits.
backbone.hardware: Laptop central processing unit would suffice, but there is nothing to embed.

integration.partner_dataset: Paleobiology Database (PBDB) occurrences plus a mammal trait resource such as the Mammal Diversity Database
integration.join_key: Genus name (free-text taxonomy, needing synonym resolution), plus latitude/longitude and age interval
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: Does adding dense low-latitude Mexican records change the dispersal and extinction rates that continental-scale fossil models infer for the Americas - a real question, but one that needs the unavailable Mexican table to answer.

controls.positive_control: Would be recovering the known ~2.8-million-year-ago dispersal pulse, which is textbook and already in the data.
controls.negative_control: Label shuffling across genera; feasible in principle but moot without the data.
controls.external_validation: PBDB occurrences for the United States and South America are open and could serve as a second source, but the paper's novel Mexican records - the entire reason to use this paper - are not in PBDB.

honest_claim_h3: At best the model could claim: among mammal genera that happen to be preserved and published from Mio-Pliocene Mexico, North America and South America, these traits predict which ones appear south of the holding pen - a claim fatally conditioned on preservation bias that the paper itself identifies as the field's central problem.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use a fossil mammal's traits and northern occurrence history to predict whether and when it spread into South America.
plain_idea.train_on: Genus-level fossil occurrence records (taxon, locality, latitude, geological age) for Mio-Pliocene Mexico, temperate North America and South America; the paper reports 5,940 such records, but the modelling unit would be the genus, of which there are only a few hundred.
plain_idea.predict: Whether a northern genus later appears in South America, and how long it lingered in the Mexican 'holding pen' first. The true answer would come from first- and last-appearance dates assembled from the same occurrence records - that is, from the features themselves.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: Paleobiogeographers debating when the Americas connected would want to know which traits predicted dispersal success; even a failure would quantify how much preservation bias limits any such inference.

more_or_better_data.why: The 1,724 Mexican genus-locality records are a genuine twofold improvement over the 919 previously available and nearly triple what PBDB holds for Mexico (639 occurrences), so the low-latitude coverage is real - but it is small in absolute terms and not obtainable.

confidence_score.why: There are no replicate measurements; the uncertainty here is age uncertainty, which the paper already handles with Bayesian occurrence-age resampling, so there is nothing an added confidence head would contribute.

models_beatable.why: The incumbent methods (DES and its 2022 trait-dependent extension, DeepDive from 2024) are purpose-built Bayesian and simulation-trained models that explicitly handle preservation bias; a generic classifier on a few hundred genera would not improve on them.

guaranteed_improvement.why: The first condition already fails: we cannot obtain the Mexican table that would be the new data, so there is no join key and no shared evaluation split.

ml_idea: Considered: predict which Mio-Pliocene North American mammal genera dispersed into South America, and the lag before they did, from body size, diet and their occurrence history in the Mexican 'holding pen'. Rejected because the label is an inference over the same occurrence records that would supply the features, the traits are absent from the data, and the data itself cannot be downloaded.

effort.compute_note: Estimated from the stated record counts only (a few thousand rows of text and numbers); nothing was timed because no file was ever obtained.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Try to download supplementary Data S1 to S8 - it takes one request, and it is what killed this: the publisher returns HTTP 403, the article has no PubMed Central copy, and no repository mirror exists.

verdict_reason: A1 fails: the dataset lives only in Science's supplementary files on a paywalled, bot-blocked site, with no Dryad, Zenodo or Paleobiology Database deposit (PBDB still shows 639 Mexican Neogene mammal occurrences against the paper's 1,724 records), so not one row could be verified. Even granting access, A2, A3 and A5 would also fail: the dispersal label would have to be inferred from the same occurrence records that provide the features, the predictive traits are not in the table, and the effective sample is a few hundred genera.
